query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating fine tungsten carbide (WC) particles into the high-entropy alloy (HEA) will yield a self-lubricating composite that exhibits significantly reduced friction and wear rates across a wide temperature range by promoting the formation of a protective, hard, and lubricious tribolayer.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional high-entropy alloy (e.g., an equiatomic AlCoCrFeNi system) with a homogeneous microstructure, exhibiting moderate intrinsic wear resistance and friction performance.
generation.intervention: Integrate an optimal fraction of tungsten carbide (WC) particles into the HEA—via methods such as powder metallurgy or laser cladding—to create a composite material.
generation.conditions: Evaluate the composite under dry sliding or lightly lubricated conditions, across a temperature range from room temperature up to approximately 800 °C, and under varying contact loads representative of self-lubricating moving components.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniform dispersion of WC particles which enhances the local hardness, refines the grain microstructure, and facilitates the in situ formation of a continuous tribolayer composed of WC fragments and partially oxidized HEA phases.
generation.mechanism: The dispersed WC particles serve as hard barriers that reduce plastic deformation and adhesion during sliding. Their presence promotes the continuous formation of a lubricious and protective tribolayer that minimizes friction and prevents severe wear, maintaining these benefits even at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the untreated HEA, the composite is expected to show a significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate (potentially reductions on the order of 60–70% as an approximate target), with performance maintained across the service temperature range.
generation.baseline: The untreated high-entropy alloy without WC reinforcement, which exhibits higher friction coefficients and wear rates under identical testing conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement will depend on ensuring optimal WC content and uniform dispersion. Excessive WC or poor interfacial bonding could lead to brittleness or phase segregation, thereby negating the tribological benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements and the precise optimal WC concentration are uncertain and must be determined experimentally; processing parameters and alloy composition may significantly influence outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the base HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi) and one set with an optimal addition of WC particles, using the same processing method (e.g., laser cladding). Subject both sample sets to controlled ball-on-disk wear tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C and under varying loads.
measurements: Coefficient of friction using a tribometer
Wear rates calculated from measured wear volumes via microscopy
Microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM, EDS) to assess WC dispersion and tribolayer formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be considered falsified if the WC-reinforced HEA does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate relative to the untreated HEA across the tested temperature range, or if detrimental microstructural inhomogeneities (e.g., clustering of WC particles leading to embrittlement) are observed.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 3A shows the Vickers hardness and wear rate variations of NiX and Ni3X as the temperature increases from RT to 800 °C. The hardness of NiX and Ni3X gradually decreases from 6.1 GPa and 4.3 GPa at RT to 3.7 GPa and 2.5 GPa at 800 °C, respectively. The high thermal hardness of NiX arises from the solid solution strengthening and the resultant heterostructures [,]. The trend in wear rate of the Ni3X with temperature is similar to that of the conventional alloys. Specifically, its wear rate increases from 1.1 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at RT to 4.2 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 600 °C, but decreases afterward to 2.4 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 800 °C. However, the wear rate of the NiX is basically maintained at the order of (10−7 to 10−6) mm3/Nm over the entire test temperature. In particular, it achieves ultra-low wear at RT (1.7 × 10−7 mm3/Nm) and 800 °C (9.1 × 10−7 mm3/Nm). Under the same dry friction conditions, the addition of an appropriate amount of WC particles can reduce the friction coefficient of the HEA matrix. In addition, the wear volume of the WC–HEA composite decreases rapidly with the increase of WC content. The wear volume of the 30 WC–HEA composite is 1.47 × 105 μm3, accounting for only 3.17% of the pure matrix material, indicating that the HEA with WC particles have better wear resistance.

Laser cladding, as an advanced method of coating preparation, can achieve metallurgical bonding between the coating material and substrate, which is important for the preparation of agricultural knives in harsh working conditions []. It has the characteristics of low dilution rate, high bonding strength, and fast solidification []. The short process time of preparing HEA by laser cladding can offset the shortcomings of the traditional methods. So, laser cladding was used in this study to prepare the HEA layer on silage knives. AlCoCrFeNi is a representative HEA system, which is considered as a kind of coating material that can be deposited on traditional alloys to improve their hardness and wear resistance []. The WC particles were added in the AlCoCrFeNi HEA, and then were coated on one side of the cutting edge of 65 Mn steel by laser cladding. The effect of WC on performance of the AlCoCrFeNi HEA coating was studied, and its microstructure, hardness and wear resistance were carefully analyzed in order to develop an alloy coating with high wear resistance.
